summary: For ages 7-9, teach complete metamorphosis in detail: egg → larva → pupa → adult, using the correct generalised terms (larva/pupa) alongside the familiar ones (caterpillar/chrysalis). The load-bearing ideas are (a) the function of each stage — the larva eats and grows, the pupa is where the body is reorganised into the adult — and (b) that many insects share this pattern, not just butterflies. Exploit how radically different the larva looks from the adult (maggot→fly, grub→beetle) to motivate 'why so different?' and prepare for incomplete metamorphosis later.
misconceptions: 'Only butterflies do metamorphosis' — beetles, flies, bees and many others share the pattern.
'The larva and adult are different animals' — they are the same individual, transformed.
'The pupa is asleep/resting' — it is actively being rebuilt inside.
'The larva just gets bigger and grows wings' — the body is reorganised, not merely enlarged.
'Caterpillar/chrysalis are the only correct words' — larva/pupa are the general terms across insects.

activities.title: Build and run the four-stage cycle, then reveal the rebuild
steps: Arrange the four stages of a butterfly's life cycle in the correct order using the proper terms: egg → larva → pupa → adult.
Examine the larva stage and state its one main job: eating and growing (shedding its skin as it swells).

Reveal what is happening inside the pupa — much of the larva's body is broken down, and groups of cells that were already in the larva build adult parts such as wings, legs and new eyes — and describe in your own words that the insect is actively rebuilt, not just enlarged or sleeping.
Run the SAME four stages for a beetle (egg → grub → pupa → beetle) and a housefly (egg → maggot → pupa → fly), and state that this is a shared insect pattern rather than a butterfly-only story.
activities.insight: Complete metamorphosis is an ordered, four-stage process shared by many insects, in which the larva's job is to eat and grow and the pupa is where the body is actively reorganised into the adult.

activities.title: Match the young to the grown-up
steps: Match each larva to the adult it becomes: maggot→fly, grub→beetle, caterpillar→butterfly.
For each pair, explain why the larva and adult look so different: the body was reorganised inside the pupa.
State that the larva and adult are the SAME individual at different stages, not two different animals.
activities.insight: The larva looks nothing like the adult because the body is rebuilt in the pupa — but it is the same insect transformed, not a separate creature.

activities.title: Which stage does which job?
steps: State the four stages in the right order: egg → larva → pupa → adult.
Say in which stage the insect does most of its eating and growing (larva) and in which stage its body is being rebuilt (pupa), and explain how you know.
Give at least two insects that undergo complete metamorphosis (e.g. butterfly and beetle).

Consider a counterexample: a grasshopper hatches as a young grasshopper (a nymph) that looks like a small adult without working wings, and it grows by shedding its skin several times, with wings developing gradually and no pupa — decide whether that is complete metamorphosis and justify your answer.
activities.insight: Understanding is shown by assigning the correct function to each stage and by recognising that an insect with no pupa (young resembling the adult) is NOT complete metamorphosis — not merely by reciting the order.

activities.title: In-role larva interview (optional engagement)
steps: Take on the role of a larva (caterpillar, grub or maggot) and answer 'What will you turn into, and how?'
Describe the stages still to come (pupa, then adult) and what happens inside the pupa.
activities.insight: Narrating the transformation from the larva's point of view can rehearse the stage order and the rebuild idea in an engaging way.

checkQuestion: A butterfly and a beetle both go through complete metamorphosis. Name the four stages in the right order, and tell me: in WHICH stage does the insect do most of its eating and growing, and in which stage is its body being rebuilt? Explain how you know.
checkAnswer: The four stages in order are: egg → larva → pupa → adult. The insect does most of its eating and growing in the LARVA stage (the caterpillar, grub or maggot — which looks completely different from the adult). The body is rebuilt in the PUPA stage (the chrysalis/cocoon), where the larva's body is reorganised into the adult. Butterflies, beetles, flies and ladybirds all go through these four stages.
